docs.title: Gitagger
docs.text:
Automate git tags without the headache. Run gitagger and it figures out your tag format, creates the next tag, and pushes it, or creates v1.0.0 for you if you have no tags yet.

gitagger                 # next patch tag, pushed if it can be
gitagger minor           # v1.2.3 -> v1.3.0
gitagger major --pre rc  # v1.2.3 -> v2.0.0-rc
gitagger --dry-run       # peek first, change nothing

docs.title: Why gitagger?
docs.text:
• Follows your convention. Triple (v1.2.3), double (v1.2), single (v7), date (v2026.10.04), even master-<sha> styles, detected from your history by majority vote. No flags needed for the common case.
  • Safe by default. Refuses to double-tag HEAD, checks the remote for collisions before pushing (with doctor), stays graceful offline, never force-pushes unless you say -f.
  • Hooks included. Run shell commands on start, success, failure, and finish: releases, notifications, whatever your flow needs.
  • One binary, everywhere. Linux, macOS, Windows, Docker, and a GitHub Action. It's a single binary with no runtime or dependencies.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• New? Install gitagger, then cut your first tag.
  • In a hurry? Commands is the full CLI reference.
  • Automating? GitHub Action, generated workflows, or Docker.
  • Something broken? FAQ & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Small Workflow Guide:
docs.text:
• always use conventional commits (conventional commit messages)

  • for non-small changes, always commit changes in parts instead of committing several hundred lines of changes and multiple file changes in one commit. (if possible or ideal) and make sure to also push them.

  • for non-small changes, always use the gh cli to execute CI jobs, and view and watch their output and progress to ensure changes come out clean. (run "gh help" for more info) you must push your changes first before using the gh cli to interact with the ci actions.

  • for mostly all changes, once comfortable with their state run the taskfile task "ops" in order to do linting and ensure that all your changes are clean, alternatively run the scripts in scripts/ops directly if needed.

  • make sure to use the build task to build after you make your changes to ensure that the binaries compile properly.

  • make sure to do testing of your changes before finalizing anything, to ensure that all works fine.

  • make sure to update docs if they are outdated.

  • make sure to always read and or briefly read the codebase and the codebases git history for your relevant (planned) changes properly before making changes in order to stay dynamic.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
No published image yet. Build it yourself (any OCI runtime: docker, podman, nerdctl…):

docker build -t gitagger .
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" -w /repo gitagger [args]

Multi-arch: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t gitagger .

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The image is non-root (gitagger user) with just git and CA certificates installed, which is all tagging needs.
  • It reads the mounted repo's .gitagger.yml like the binary does; all flags work the same.
  • Match host file ownership with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)", and make sure the mounted directory is readable by the container user.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# peek at the plan
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" -w /repo gitagger --dry-run

# tag without pushing
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" -w /repo gitagger --no-push

# inspect
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" -w /repo gitagger list

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Tag from CI with the marketplace action:

- uses: CHE3MZ/gitagger@v1

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Default Meaning args "" Extra args passed to gitagger, e.g. "minor --pre rc" version latest gitagger release to use (v1.0.2, or latest) working-directory . Directory to run gitagger in token github.token Token for release API calls (higher rate limits)

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Output Meaning tag Tag now pointing at HEAD (empty when none)

docs.title: Example: manual bump choice
docs.text:
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: 'Tag bump type'
        required: false
        default: 'patch'
        type: choice
        options:
          - patch
          - minor
          - major
jobs:
  tag:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: CHE3MZ/gitagger@v1
        with:
          args: ${{ inputs.bump }}

History matters

Auto-detect needs history, so check out with fetch-depth: 0. The action fetches tags itself as best effort, but a full clone is the reliable setup. The action runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows runners.

docs.title: Generated workflows
docs.text:
Don't hand-write CI. Generate it:

gitagger workflow             # overview
gitagger workflow --list      # available presets
gitagger workflow init gh     # .github/workflows/gitagger.yml
gitagger workflow init jenkins  # .jenkins/gitagger.jenkinsfile

Add -f to overwrite, -p <dir> to generate elsewhere. Generation also ensures a .gitagger.yml exists (writing the default one if missing) without touching an existing config.

docs.title: GitHub (gh)
docs.text: Tags on workflow_dispatch using the gitagger action. Needs contents: write, a full checkout (fetch-depth: 0), and a git identity, all included in the template. Extend it with dispatch inputs as shown in GitHub Action.

docs.title: Jenkins (jenkins)
docs.text:
Tags via go install plus gitagger, with the git identity configured. Runs wherever your agent runs.

Gitea / Forgejo

Gitea Actions (and Forgejo) speak GitHub-compatible workflow YAML, so the gh template works there as-is.

docs.title: Your first tag
docs.text:
You need a git repo with at least one commit. Then:

cd your-project
gitagger --dry-run

Dry-run prints the plan and changes nothing:

dry run — nothing created
next: v1.0.0  (triple, stable)
would push to origin

No tags yet? gitagger starts you at v1.0.0. Already have tags? It detects your format (triple, double, single, date, sha…) and the v prefix from history and follows them. Happy with the plan? Run it for real:

gitagger

That creates the tag and pushes it to origin when it can (no remote or offline? it keeps the tag locally and tells you how to push later).

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Run gitagger init once to write a .gitagger.yml, tweak it, then forget about flags: bare gitagger uses your config from then on. See Configuration.

docs.title: Useful next commands
docs.text:
gitagger list        # all tags, oldest first
gitagger view v1.0.0  # details for one tag
gitagger check -v    # is my config valid?
gitagger doctor      # local vs remote tag health
gitagger --help      # everything else

Full reference: Commands.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Pick whichever fits. They all give you the same gitagger binary.

docs.title: Go
docs.text:
go install github.com/CHE3MZ/gitagger/cmd/gitagger@latest

Requires Go 1.26 or newer.

docs.title: Prebuilt binaries
docs.text: Grab one from the releases page: Linux, macOS, and Windows, on amd64 and arm64.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/CHE3MZ/gitagger.git
cd gitagger
go build -o gitagger ./cmd/gitagger

Requires Go 1.26 or newer.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
No published image yet. Build it yourself (any OCI runtime: docker, podman, nerdctl…):

docker build -t gitagger .
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" -w /repo gitagger [args]

Match host file ownership with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)". The mounted directory must be readable by the container user.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
- uses: CHE3MZ/gitagger@v1

See the GitHub Actions guide for inputs (args, version, working-directory) and details.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Cut your first tag.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Short version: small branches, green CI, conventional titles, human review. The full process (local gates, what to run before pushing, ground rules) is in CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo.

Make sure every workflow is green before opening the PR (gh run watch), and never cut tags or releases: the maintainer handles all of that.

docs.title: It says "already on vX"
docs.text: HEAD already has a tag. That's the double-tag guard. Make a new commit, or retag deliberately with -f.

docs.title: It says the tag "already exists on remote"
docs.text: Someone (or a previous run) already pushed that tag. gitagger doctor shows local-only vs remote-only tags. Overwrite only if you mean it (-f force-pushes).

docs.title: It refuses to move a float backwards
docs.text: release-action.sh only moves vX / vX.Y forward. If it refuses, the new tag doesn't descend from the floats, usually a rewound or stale history. Don't force it blindly: verify the new tip contains everything (git diff <float> <tip> --stat), then move floats by hand with git tag -f + git push --force. Stop rewriting public history; merge forward instead.

docs.title: It kept the tag locally
docs.text: No remote (no remote "origin") or unreachable remote (offline?): the tag is created, just not pushed. Run the printed git push <remote> <tag> later.

docs.title: It tagged nothing on a release commit
docs.text: This is correct behavior: release commits already carry tags, so gitagger aborts instead of double-tagging. The action's self-test hits this on purpose and probes a fresh commit instead.

docs.title: My format wasn't detected
docs.text: Unknown tag styles are ignored; with no recognizable tags gitagger starts at triple. Force a style with --format, or set format: in config. doctor lists "odd tags" it skipped.

docs.title: Config ignored?
docs.text: gitagger check -v shows the resolved values and the file they came from. Flags beat config, and the file is looked up in the working directory (-p / working-directory / -w change where that is).

docs.title: Typo'd command?
docs.text: hlp and friends get a did-you-mean suggestion with exit code 3. Gibberish gets none.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue with NO_COLOR=1 gitagger check -v output, your .gitagger.yml (secrets redacted), and the exact command plus its output.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command supports -h / --help. Unknown flags are always an error naming the right help text. Typo a command and gitagger suggests the closest match:

error: don't know what "hlp" means — try `gitagger --help`

The most similar command is
        help

Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 runtime error, 2 already-exists / no-op, 3 bad arguments.

docs.title: Tagging
docs.text:
Command What it does gitagger Next tag from config (default: patch bump), pushed when possible gitagger patch Bump 0.0.X gitagger minor Bump 0.X.0 gitagger major Bump X.0.0

Common flags: --pre rc|beta|build|nightly, --format auto|triple|double|single|date|sha|sha-num, -m "message" (annotated tag), -n keep local, -d dry-run, -f force, -r abort on dirty tree, -v verbose, -p <dir> operate elsewhere, -a <name> hook arguments. See Tagging.

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text: Command What it does next [scale] The tag the next real run would create (creates nothing) list (ls) All tags, oldest first view <tag> Name, type (annotated/lightweight), message, commit, date check [-v] Is .gitagger.yml valid? (-v shows resolved values) doctor [-v] Local vs remote tag health: odd styles, local-only/remote-only tags, HEAD distance

docs.title: Removing
docs.text: Command What it does remove <tag> (rm) Asks are you sure…? [y/n], then deletes locally and on the remote when present remove <tag> -c Remove without asking remove <tag> -n Remove only the local tag, keep the remote one

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Command What it does test [--keep] Clone to a temp sandbox (remotes stripped), run the full tag flow with hooks, print results, delete the sandbox

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Command What it does init [-f] [--comment] [-p] Write .gitagger.yml without comments (refuses to overwrite without -f; --comment writes it with the full comments) remote <name> Save another push remote into the config remote --show Show the current remote URL workflow Generate CI workflow files (see Workflows) handbook Print the .gitagger.yml handbook help [command] This reference, per command version Build version

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
gitagger init writes a .gitagger.yml (recognized siblings: .gitagger.yaml, .gitagger; first found wins). Everything is optional. Precedence: flags > config > defaults. Run gitagger check -v to see the resolved values, or gitagger handbook for this same reference in your terminal.

# Tag size for triple/double/single styles.
scale: patch            # major | minor | patch

# Flavor appended to the tag. stable = no suffix.
pre: stable              # stable | rc | beta | build | nightly

# Tag style. auto follows your tag history.
format: auto              # auto | triple | double | single | date | sha | sha-num | custom

# Custom template. Only used when format is custom.
custom: ""                # e.g. "build-<SHA>-v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH>-<DATE><PRE>"

# Push target. Must exist for auto-push to happen.
remote: origin

# Auto-push the new tag when the remote is reachable.
push: true                # false keeps tags local (same as -n)

# Always overwrite clashing tags and force-push them.
force: false              # same as -f on every run. Keep false unless you mean it.

# Abort instead of tagging when the working tree is dirty.
require_clean: false

# Pre-tag remote check. Aborts early on collision.
doctor: false

# Show detection details and the plan while working.
verbose: false            # same as -v on every run

# Tag message. Empty output = lightweight tag; text = annotated tag.
# Text form is literal. Command form runs shell commands and joins
# their output with newlines; a failing command aborts before tagging.
message:
  cmds:
    - cmd: echo ""
# EXAMPLE: message: { cmds: [ "echo one", { cmd: "echo two", shell: bash, os: linux, macos } ] }

# Operate in another directory (same as -p).
path: ""

# Hooks: shell commands at lifecycle events. See Hooks.
on:
  failure:
    - shell: sh
      os: macos, linux
      run:
        - echo "Oops! Something went wrong..."
    - shell: pwsh
      os: windows
      run:
        - echo "Oops! Something went wrong..."

Strict but forgiving

Unknown config keys are an error (typos under known sections too), except retired keys (version:, confirm:), which still load fine. A broken config aborts before anything mutates; a missing file just means defaults.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Shell commands at lifecycle events: start runs first, success after tagging and pushing, failure on errors, finish always (both outcomes). Each event takes one block or a list of blocks.

on:
  success:
    - shell: sh
      os: linux, macos
      run:
        - echo "tagged $GITAGGER_TAG"
    - shell: pwsh
      os: windows
      run: echo "tagged $GITAGGER_TAG"

docs.title: Block keys
docs.text: Key Meaning run: One command or a list. Each item runs separately. Required. shell: sh, bash, pwsh, batch (= cmd /C, Windows only). Default on unix: sh -c (POSIX-guaranteed, no fallback); on Windows: pwsh, then Windows PowerShell, then cmd, then bash. pwsh on Windows follows that same chain; sh/bash run exactly as named. os: linux, macos, windows. Default: all. Comma lists work (os: macos, linux). argument: Block runs only with gitagger -a <name>. Special values: none (only when no -a given), any (only when some -a given).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Every hook gets:

Variable Contents GITAGGER_TAG The new tag GITAGGER_PREV The previous tag (empty on first tag) GITAGGER_REMOTE The push remote GITAGGER_PUSHED true/false GITAGGER_DRY_RUN true inside gitagger test, false otherwise GITAGGER_EVENT The lifecycle event GITAGGER_ARGUMENT Comma-joined -a values

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
A failing success hook still runs the failure hooks first (try/catch/finally), then reports the original error. The failed tag does not survive: it is removed locally, and a tag pushed by this run is removed from the remote too (an overwritten remote tag is restored instead). A failing failure/finish hook is reported, never re-triggered; hooks can't loop forever.

Changelogs and releases

Hooks compose with outside tools: run your release script or changelog generator as a success hook (it gets $GITAGGER_TAG and friends) instead of asking gitagger to own changelogs.

docs.title: How the next tag is chosen
docs.text:
1. Format. --format wins; otherwise auto detects it from your last 20 tags by majority vote (ties go to the newest). Fresh repos start at triple with a v prefix.
  2. Previous tag. The highest version in that format (not just the newest date; back-tagged histories are handled).
  3. Bump. major/minor/patch from the command line, falling back to config, defaulting to patch.
  4. Flavor. --pre (or config): stable means no suffix; otherwise -rc, -beta, -build, -nightly. Promoting v1.2.4-rc to stable yields v1.2.4 (no bump); switching flavors swaps the suffix.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Format Looks like Bumps triple v1.2.3 Per scale double v1.2 major bumps major, else minor single v7 Any scale bumps the number date v2026.10.04 Today's date (.N on collision) sha master-abc1234 Current short SHA sha-num master-99-abc1234 Commit count + short SHA custom Your template Config only (see below)

The v prefix follows your history: keep it if most tags have it.

docs.title: Custom format (config only)
docs.text:
Set format: custom plus a custom: template. Tokens: MAJOR MINOR PATCH YEAR MONTH DAY DATE SHA FULLSHA COUNT PRE NUMBER TAG.

format: custom
custom: "build-<SHA>-v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH>-<DATE><PRE>"

No auto-detect for custom; explicit is on purpose.

docs.title: Safety rails
docs.text:
• HEAD already tagged → aborts (exit 2) unless -f.
  • Tag exists locally or remotely → aborts unless -f (and never silently overwrites a push).
  • Dirty tree → warns and continues, unless require_clean is set (then it aborts).
  • No remote / offline → keeps the tag locally and tells you the exact git push to run later.
  • --dry-run → prints the plan, changes nothing. Use it liberally.
  • doctor: true → checks the remote for collisions before creating the tag, so a doomed tag never gets created locally.
  • Failing success hooks → the tag is rolled back locally and removed from the remote (an overwritten tag is restored instead); nothing broken survives.
  • --unsafe / unsafe: true → escape hatch: skips the aborts above, skips rollback, pushes anyway, and warns loudly. Not written by init; add it by hand.
